package_info.package_manager: Linux (malware distributed as shell scripts, binaries, and Perl scripts)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware campaign, not a versioned package)
package_info.why_malicious: This campaign is malicious because it orchestrates a multi-stage attack involving brute-force SSH access, deployment of downloader scripts, installation and execution of the XMRig cryptocurrency miner, and activation of a Perl-based IRC DDoS bot. The malware abuses system resources for illicit mining, establishes persistent remote control via IRC, and enables attackers to launch DDoS attacks, all without user consent or awareness.

execution_context.trigger: post-compromise (immediately after successful SSH brute-force attack)
execution_context.file_location: Downloader shell script (e.g., kermine, run, .b4nd1d0) located in /tmp or home directory

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After post-compromise, the script downloads a tar archive from a remote attacker-controlled server using wget, extracts its contents to /tmp, sets execute permissions on the extracted xmrig binary, and immediately executes the miner, resulting in unauthorized code execution and system resource hijacking.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script performs an automated download and execution of a binary from an untrusted external IP address, a hallmark of malware delivery and lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate post-authentication scripts do not fetch and execute remote binaries, especially cryptocurrency miners, without explicit user action and from non-standard locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: DevOps or system automation scripts may download and install software, but only from trusted repositories and with user awareness; such scripts are typically version-controlled and auditable.
key_indicators: Use of wget or curl to download files from suspicious or hardcoded IP addresses
Immediate execution of newly downloaded binaries
Staging and execution of binaries from /tmp or hidden directories
Lack of user interaction or notification during execution

execution_context.file_location: Extracted binary (/tmp/xmrig, /tmp/.system3d, or similar in /tmp or hidden directories)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the xmrig binary is executed with a configuration file located in /tmp, causing the process to hijack system CPU resources for Monero mining and transmit mining results to a remote mining pool controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited execution of cryptocurrency mining software in non-standard locations is a clear indicator of resource hijacking malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not mine cryptocurrency or consume excessive CPU resources without explicit user consent and proper installation procedures.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Cryptocurrency mining software is legitimate only when knowingly installed and configured by the system owner, typically in standard directories and with user awareness.
key_indicators: Presence of xmrig or similar mining binaries in /tmp or hidden directories
Mining configuration files (e.g., config.json) located in /tmp or non-standard paths
High, sustained CPU usage by unknown or suspicious processes
Outbound network connections to known mining pool addresses

execution_context.file_location: Perl script (e.g., botcarternew, .ubuntu) located in /tmp or home directory

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Perl script initiates an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled IRC server, joins a specific channel, and listens for remote DDoS commands, enabling the compromised host to participate in coordinated DDoS attacks as part of a botnet.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated IRC connections and command execution for DDoS attacks are classic behaviors of botnet malware, especially when initiated by hidden or unauthorized scripts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Perl scripts do not establish persistent IRC connections or await remote attack commands without user intent or business justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IRC bots may be used for legitimate chat automation or monitoring, but not for DDoS or remote attack orchestration.
key_indicators: Outbound IRC connections from server processes or Perl scripts
Perl scripts containing DDoS routines or command-and-control logic
Persistence mechanisms to relaunch bot scripts after reboot
Unusual network activity to IRC ports (e.g., 6667) from non-user processes

attack_chain.action: Brute-force SSH credentials to gain unauthorized access to Linux servers.
Deploy and execute downloader shell script to fetch additional payloads from remote servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Download and execution of miner and bot binaries

attack_chain.action: Extract and execute XMRig miner to hijack system resources for cryptocurrency mining.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing illicit mining and resource abuse

attack_chain.action: Deploy and execute Perl DDoS IRC bot to connect to attacker-controlled IRC channels for remote command and control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Botnet participation and DDoS attack capability

behavioral_signatures: Automated download and execution of binaries from remote, non-standard URLs or hardcoded IP addresses
Presence and execution of XMRig miner or similar binaries in /tmp or hidden directories
Creation or use of mining configuration files (e.g., config.json) in /tmp or non-standard locations
Outbound IRC connections from non-user or Perl script processes
High, sustained CPU usage by unknown or suspicious processes
Persistence mechanisms for malicious scripts or binaries
network_indicators: Outbound IRC traffic to attacker-controlled servers (e.g., on port 6667)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized SSH logins followed by the download and execution of binaries from suspicious external URLs or hardcoded IP addresses. Detect the presence of XMRig or similar mining binaries and configuration files in temporary or hidden directories. Alert on outbound IRC connections from server or Perl script processes, especially to non-standard destinations or ports. Correlate high, sustained CPU usage with the presence of these indicators to identify illicit mining activity. Look for persistence mechanisms that relaunch malicious scripts or binaries after reboot.
